title: The Best Safety Apps for Solo Travellers in 2026
description: An honest comparison of solo travel safety apps: Life360, bSafe, Noonlight, TripWhistle, government registration services and roammate. What each one actually does, and where each one stops working.
intro: Most safety app roundups list ten apps as if they were interchangeable. They are not. They do three different jobs: letting people you trust see where you are, getting help from local emergency services quickly, and reducing the chance of ending up somewhere isolated with someone you have only just met. No single app covers all three, and several of the best known ones only work properly in one country. This comparison goes app by app and says plainly where each one stops being useful, including ours, which sits in a different category from the rest and is easy to mistake for a tracker.

sections.heading: Life360: best for continuous location sharing with people who already know you
sections.content: Life360 is a location-sharing app built around Circles: a group of people who can see each other's live position on a map, with arrival and departure alerts for saved places. It was designed for families rather than travellers, and that shows in the best way. It is one of the few apps where sharing your position for weeks on end is the normal use case rather than an emergency mode. For a solo traveller, the realistic setup is a Circle of two or three people at home who can see which city you are in and whether you got back to your accommodation. It runs on GPS plus a data connection, so it works wherever your phone does, but it needs background location permission and a live eSIM or roaming plan to be worth anything. The paid tiers add features like crash detection and roadside assistance; check the current tier list in the store, because it changes. Its limitation is blunt: Life360 tells people something is wrong. It does not tell anyone who can help.

sections.heading: bSafe: best for a live guardian on one specific journey
sections.content: bSafe works at a smaller scale than Life360, and that is the point. You nominate guardians, and then you activate protection for a single trip: the walk back from a bar, a taxi from the airport, a first meeting with someone you matched with online. An SOS alarm notifies your guardians with your location, and the app can stream audio and video to them so there is a record of what happened rather than just a pin on a map. There is also a timed check-in: if you do not confirm you are safe by the time you set, the alarm fires on its own. That timed pattern is the single most useful mechanism in this entire category, because it protects you in the case where you are unable to press anything. What bSafe cannot do is contact emergency services on your behalf. Your guardians receive the alert, and what happens next depends entirely on whether they are awake, in signal, and know what your local emergency number is. Choose guardians in a helpful time zone.

sections.heading: Noonlight: best in the United States, and effectively nowhere else
sections.content: Noonlight is the app most often recommended without the caveat that matters most. You hold a button; releasing it without entering your PIN triggers a silent alarm, and Noonlight's dispatch centre passes your location to emergency responders. It is genuinely excellent, and it is built on the United States emergency dispatch system. Outside the US that dispatch chain does not exist, so the part of the product you actually installed it for is the part that does not travel with you. Treat it as a domestic tool. This is the general trap in the safety app category: anything that promises to send help, rather than to send a message, is wired into one country's emergency infrastructure. Before you rely on any app with a dispatch feature abroad, open its own coverage or FAQ page and confirm the country you are going to is listed. If the answer is unclear, assume it does not work there. An app you believe will summon an ambulance and will not is worse than no app at all, because you have planned around it.

sections.heading: TripWhistle: best for finding the emergency number you do not know
sections.content: There is no international 911. Emergency numbers differ by country and sometimes by service: police, ambulance and fire are three separate numbers in a lot of places, and the number you memorised at home will connect you to nothing. TripWhistle exists for exactly that gap: it holds emergency numbers by country and service, and it will give you your GPS coordinates in a format you can text to someone or read aloud to a dispatcher who has no idea where you are. That second feature is underrated. The hardest part of an emergency call in an unfamiliar city is not the language, it is describing a location you cannot name. It is a reference tool, not an alarm (nobody is notified when you open it), and like every reference tool, its value depends on you knowing it is installed. Screenshot the numbers for your destination before you arrive so the information survives a dead battery, a lost phone, or no signal at all.

sections.heading: Government registration and advisory apps: best for the emergencies no app can fix
sections.content: Most foreign ministries run some combination of a travel advisory service and a registration scheme that tells your embassy you are in the country. The United States State Department's STEP programme is the best known; Australia's Smartraveller and equivalent services elsewhere publish country advisories you can subscribe to. Provision varies a lot by nationality (some governments run a full registration database, others only publish alerts), so check what your own foreign ministry actually offers rather than assuming a friend's setup applies to you. These are not personal safety apps and they will not help you on a dark street. They matter for the category of emergency the consumer apps ignore entirely: a coup, a natural disaster, an evacuation, a lost passport, a hospital admission where somebody needs to reach your family. Registration is a two-minute task with a very long tail of usefulness, and it is free. Do it alongside forwarding your insurance policy number and passport scan to someone at home.

sections.heading: roammate: companion matching with SOS contacts, not a location tracker
sections.content: roammate belongs in a different row of this table, and it is worth being clear about why. It is not a personal safety tracker and it does not compete with Life360. It is a travel companion matching app: it pairs travellers on travel style, daily budget bracket and destination overlap, so that the person you end up spending a day with is someone whose plans actually fit yours. The safety mechanisms are built around that. You nominate emergency contacts in the app, and you can raise an SOS alert to them. Conversations happen in in-app chat before anyone meets, and block and report are available on every profile and conversation. Nobody sees your live position on a map. The honest framing is preventative rather than reactive: the main safety contribution is not travelling alone by default, and knowing something about who you are meeting before you meet them. roammate is free on iOS and Android, with no premium tier and no ads. If what you want is continuous location sharing with your family, install Life360 as well. The two are not substitutes.

sections.heading: How to stack them without carrying five apps
sections.content: A workable setup is three apps and one habit. One continuous sharer, set up before you leave and left running: Life360 or your phone's built-in location sharing, which costs nothing and is already installed. One trip-level alarm with named guardians, used deliberately on the journeys that warrant it rather than permanently. One reference for local emergency numbers, screenshotted for offline access. Add embassy registration for the country if your government offers it. The habit does more than any of them: before a meetup or a night out, send someone the plan: where, who, and roughly when you expect to be back. Every app in this comparison is a delivery mechanism for that message; sending it yourself needs no battery, no data and no subscription. Then check the boring things. Background location permission actually granted, battery bank charged, a data plan that works on arrival rather than after you find wifi. A safety app with no signal and eight percent battery is not a safety app.
